analysis.one_liner: Requires companies that sell Americans' personal data to safeguard it, correct errors, and face lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on a bill to regulate data brokers, introduced after a breach exposed hundreds of thousands of consumer profiles; it died in subcommittee in the 109th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Federal Trade Commission to write rules for "information brokers" — companies that compile and sell Americans' personal data. The rules would have required these firms to keep their databases accurate, verify who is buying the data, track every access, protect the information from theft, and let individuals see their own files, learn who purchased them, and fix errors. It would have let the FTC, state attorneys general, and individuals themselves sue to enforce those rules, and it left stronger state privacy laws in place.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers whose names, Social Security numbers, and financial data sit in data brokers' commercial databases would gain rights to see who bought their information, correct errors, and sue for up to $1,000 per violation, plus protection from the identity theft that the FTC said hit 10 million Americans in 2004. [S2] [S3]

how_it_helps.text: Gives individuals the right to see the personal data a broker holds on them, learn the identity of every entity that purchased it, and get prompt correction of errors — the bill's findings note that wrong information can cost people jobs, credit, housing, and insurance. [S2] [S3]

Requires brokers to safeguard data, authenticate users, track every access and its purpose, and detect and mitigate unauthorized access — a direct response to the 2004 breach in which a fraud operation obtained hundreds of thousands of profiles from one large information broker. [S2] [S3]

Creates real enforcement teeth: violations count as unfair or deceptive practices under the FTC Act, state attorneys general can sue for damages and restitution on behalf of residents, and individuals can recover actual losses or up to $1,000 per violation. [S2] [S3]
Leaves stronger state privacy laws fully in place, so the federal rules would have been a floor, not a ceiling. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Information brokers — companies like ChoicePoint and LexisNexis that compile and sell Americans' personal profiles — would bear the cost of building the required security, accuracy, and access systems, and would face FTC penalties, state lawsuits, and private suits of up to $1,000 per violation when they failed. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers and companies selling personal data

drawbacks.text: The private right of action allows up to $1,000 per violation, which critics of similar bills argued could invite costly class litigation whose expenses brokers would pass on to customers and, ultimately, consumers. [S3]

HHanding the FTC broad rulemaking power over a poorly defined category — 'any personal information which may be used to identify a person' — with broad authority to exempt companies could produce slow, uneven rules depending on which administration enforced them. [S3]

Compliance costs would fall hardest on smaller brokers, and the bill's findings acknowledge that both individuals and businesses bear the $52.6 billion annual identity-theft burden, so some costs are unavoidable either way. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to ordinary people is concrete and large: identity theft was already the most common fraud in America, hitting 10 million people and costing $52.6 billion in 2004, and the bill would have given consumers the same visibility and correction rights over data brokers that credit law gives them over credit bureaus. The costs — compliance spending by brokers and possible litigation — are real but modest by comparison, and the bill was carefully drawn to exempt firms whose data handling is incidental to their main business and to preserve stronger state laws. The main weakness is reliance on FTC rulemaking, which could have been slow or laxly enforced.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee from March 2005 onward and never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 3, 2005, days after Congress learned that a massive breach at a large information broker had exposed hundreds of thousands of individual profiles, a fact the bill itself cites. [S3] [S5]
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and, on March 14, 2005, to its Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection. [S5]
No further action was ever recorded: no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Information brokers came out ahead: they kept compiling and selling personal profiles for two more years with no federal accuracy, security, or disclosure requirements. Consumers whose data was sold — including people whose information was exposed in the 2005 broker breaches — remained without the access, correction, and enforcement rights the bill would have created.

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly all Democratic: 21 of the 23 cosponsors were Democrats, with 1 Republican and 1 independent, and the Republican-run committee never acted on the bill. [S4] [S5]

industries.note: The bill's whole purpose was to impose accuracy, security, tracking, and disclosure duties on firms whose business is compiling and selling personal profiles, with FTC enforcement and private lawsuits attached. Compliance costs and liability fell directly on them, and their unregulated sale of personal data is what the bill targeted.

Credit bureaus and similar firms already governed by the Fair Credit Reporting Act would have had to comply with both laws, whichever gave greater protection. The bill did not replace the FCRA regime that keeps these firms central to Americans' credit lives.
